title: Demonstrate an understanding of the grain handling industry

lessons.title: Grain in South Africa
lessons.html:
Grain in South Africa

Grain feeds the country. Bread, mealie meal, samp, breakfast cereal, cooking oil and animal feed all come from grain. Grain handling is the work of receiving, storing, looking after and sending out grain so it stays safe and good to eat.

Main grains and oilseeds

CropMain use
White maizeMealie meal and samp for people
Yellow maizeAnimal feed for chickens, pigs and cattle
WheatFlour for bread and baking
SorghumPorridge, traditional beer, feed
BarleyMalt for beer
SunflowerCooking oil, and oilcake for feed
SoybeansOil and protein for animal feed
GroundnutsPeanut butter and snacks

Maize is the biggest crop. Much of it is grown in the Free State, Mpumalanga and North West. Most summer crops are harvested from about April to July. Wheat is a winter crop, grown mostly in the Western Cape and Free State.

The grain chain

  1. Farmer plants and harvests the crop.
  2. Silo or storage company receives, weighs, grades, stores and dispatches the grain.
  3. Trader or buyer buys the grain from the farmer.
  4. Miller or processor makes it into meal, flour, oil or feed.
  5. Shop sells the food to people.

Some grain is also exported to other countries, and some is imported when South Africa does not grow enough, for example wheat.

You work in the second link of this chain. If grain is spoilt at the silo, the miller, the shop and the family at home all lose. If grain is lost or mixed up, the farmer is not paid fairly for a whole year of work.

lessons.title: How silos work and your role
lessons.html:
How silos work

A silo site has tall bins (concrete or steel), sometimes also bunkers and sheds. Grain is moved by conveyors, elevators (bucket elevators) and augers. The main work areas are:

  • Weighbridge: weighs trucks full and empty.
  • Sampling and grading: takes a sample and decides the grade and moisture.
  • Intake: grain is tipped into pits and moved to bins.
  • Storage: grain is kept cool, dry and free of insects.
  • Dispatch: grain is loaded onto trucks or rail trucks for buyers.
  • Office: keeps records of who owns which grain.

Grading

Every load is graded. The grade depends on things like moisture, broken grain, foreign matter, insects and defects. Grading rules are set under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990. Grade decides the price.

Organisations in the industry

  • Grain SA: an organisation that represents grain farmers.
  • SAGIS (South African Grain Information Service): collects figures on how much grain is delivered, stored and used.
  • JSE: the Johannesburg Stock Exchange has a market where grain prices are set by buyers and sellers.

Quality and safety

Grain must stay safe to eat. This means no mould, no poison, no chemicals beyond limits, no glass or metal. Workers keep grain safe by keeping it clean and dry, keeping grades apart, and following pest control rules.

Silo work also has dangers: dust explosions, falls from heights, being buried in grain, and moving machines. Everyone must follow the safety rules.

Your role

Every worker matters: the sampler, the weighbridge clerk, the intake operator, the cleaner. Doing your job well keeps grain safe, farmers paid fairly and the business going.

Key points

  • Maize is South Africa's biggest grain crop; white maize feeds people, yellow maize feeds animals.
  • The grain chain goes from farmer to silo, trader, miller and shop.
  • Silos weigh, sample, grade, store and dispatch grain.
  • Grade decides the price and is set by official grading rules.
  • Clean, dry, separate grain and safe work keep the chain going.
